tweets.text:
Baidu's new AI just spent 11 hours building a video game.

A full third-person martial arts game in Unreal Engine 5.8.

It's called Yunxiu Journey. Misty sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie, an ancient temple on a cliff, wuxia combat. Built by ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview.

Here's the part that got me:

ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a text-only model. It can't see the screen.

So when playtesting turned up characters floating in midair, running in the wrong direction, cameras sitting in the wrong spot... it couldn't just look and fix it.

Instead it turned every visual bug into a code problem it could measure. Write a test. Run it. Check the numbers. Fix. Run again.

That's how a senior engineer debugs something they can't eyeball.

Over those 11 hours it:
• Pulled assets from multiple generations of Unreal Engine into one UE5.8 project
• Wrote the entire game in C++
• Kept testing, debugging and iterating until the game hit its goal

This is the shift I keep talking about.

Most people still use AI to write snippets.

Autocomplete with extra steps.

The models that matter now can hold a messy project for half a day, break things, notice, and fix them without you babysitting.

Specs for the nerds:
• 280B total parameters, 14B active per token
• 1M token context window
• 200+ tokens per second
• Optimized for Unreal, Unity and Godot

And the coding benchmarks are looking promising too.

On https://t.co/FsasFjIqkD Code Arena: WebDev, ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview scored 1,668 points, just two points behind Qwen3.8-Max at 1,670. It's now trending toward becoming the #2 open model on the leaderboard.

The API is live now on Baidu's Qianfan platform.
And the weights are scheduled to go open source before November 25.

An 11-hour game dev run from a model you'll soon be able to download yourself.

Turns out, the impressive part isn't getting AI to write the game. It's getting AI to finish it.

tweets.text:
The leading dictation product still needs a qualifying correction on roughly one in five drafts in this test. That is a more useful starting point for a product roadmap than declaring dictation solved.

Wispr reaches 79.4% zero-edit rate in @voicearena_ai's scripted US-English, macOS evaluation. The LLM-judged metric focuses on corrections under a published content rubric, not perfect punctuation or formatting, so the remaining 20.6% is not simply a collection of cosmetic preferences.

For builders, the next question should be what remains in those drafts. Wrong names, missing content and unwanted generated text suggest different fixes; they should not disappear inside an average.

That is what makes the depth of this release valuable. The whitepaper goes beyond naming the leader and provides examples, use-case breakdowns and scoring rules that help explain what still needs work.

A good result should make the next engineering challenge clearer, not make it invisible. This benchmark gives the industry a way to discuss progress in terms of the corrections still left for the user, rather than treating a strong aggregate score as the end of the problem.
